topic.subject: science
topic.title: Motion and measurement of distances
topic.scope: standard units, SI units, measuring length correctly, types of motion (straight-line, circular, periodic)

misconceptions.statement: Using body parts like handspans is a perfectly accurate way to measure length.
misconceptions.why: Students rely on their own bodies as the most immediate and accessible measuring tools in daily life.
misconceptions.fix: Body parts vary in size from person to person, so they cannot provide a consistent or standard measurement for everyone.

probe.question: If you and your friend measure the same table using handspans, will you get the same number?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because a handspan is a fixed unit of length.

misconceptions.statement: You must always start measuring from the very edge of the ruler.
misconceptions.why: Students often confuse the physical edge of the scale with the zero mark.
misconceptions.fix: Measurement should start from the zero mark, as the edge of the scale might be broken or worn out.

probe.question: If the zero mark on your scale is broken, how do you measure an object?
probe.wrong_answer: I cannot measure it because the scale is broken at the start.

misconceptions.statement: An object moving in a circle is not changing its position.
misconceptions.why: Students often equate 'motion' only with moving from one place to another in a straight line.
misconceptions.fix: Motion is any change in position over time, regardless of whether the path is straight or curved.

probe.question: Is a stone tied to a string and whirled around in a circle in motion?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because it stays in the same area and doesn't go anywhere.

misconceptions.statement: Periodic motion must always involve a back-and-forth movement.
misconceptions.why: Students often overgeneralize the example of a pendulum to all periodic motions.
misconceptions.fix: Periodic motion is any motion that repeats itself at regular intervals, such as the rotation of the Earth or a fan blade.

probe.question: Is the motion of the blades of a ceiling fan periodic?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because it does not move back and forth like a pendulum.
